titulo: How they talk when it isn't to you
subtitulo: A taco stand at ten at night, at the speed it actually runs, and half the sentences in there are ones you already own
cena: Two regulars are ordering past you at a busy taco stand, and neither sentence has all its letters left in it — and none of it is slowed down for you.
frasePiso: If all you take from this part is that 'está' can shrink to 'tá, you will already follow more of a real conversation than most visitors ever do.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: In fast, informal Mexican Spanish, common reductions include está to 'tá, para to pa', nada to na', and pues to pos or pus; the intervocalic d in -ado/-ada endings also commonly drops in relaxed speech (cansado to cansao). None of this is an error — it is ordinary rapid colloquial speech.
fatosDatados.fonte: Consenso de fontes linguísticas (SoundCy; Tandem; StudySmarter — elision in Spanish)

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Mexican Spanish varies noticeably by region: the speech of central Mexico (including Mexico City) tends to be fast and clipped, coastal varieties like Veracruz have a more sing-song rhythm, Yucatecan Spanish carries Maya-influenced vocabulary and intonation, and northern varieties show a distinctive accent with some English influence near the border.
fatosDatados.fonte: Consenso de fontes linguísticas (The Spanish Group; descrições dialetais regionais)

steps.pt: Today trains your ear, not your mouth. Fast, informal Mexican Spanish drops sounds constantly — and you already own most of it.
So say nothing for the next few minutes. The exercise today is entirely your ears.
Ten at night, a busy taco stand. Two regulars order back to back, and neither sentence slows down for you.

steps.es: ¿Me da dos de pastor y uno de bistec, pa' llevar?
steps.pt: 👂 Not for you. Nothing to work out — let it go past.
steps.tts: ¿Me da dos de pastor y uno de bistec, pa' llevar?

steps.pt: 👂 Still not for you. Nothing to do yet.
You didn't catch that, and your ear is fine — every pattern in it comes slowed down next.
First pattern, and the most common: está shrinks to 'tá. Here it is in full, the way you learned it.
👂 Yours, from part eight. Every syllable in place.
👂 Same question, same bathroom. 'Está' lost its front half and nobody noticed but you.
Second: para shrinks to pa' — you asked this exact question in part seventeen, at the pharmacy.
👂 Yours, careful and complete.
👂 One syllable lighter, same question, same pharmacist.
Third: nada shrinks to na' — you said this about a peanut allergy. It matters more than most.

steps.es: No puedo comer nada que contenga cacahuate.
steps.pinyin: noh PWEH-doh koh-MEHR NAH-dah keh kohn-TEN-gah kah-kah-WAH-teh
steps.pt: 👂 Yours, from part thirteen. Full and clear.
steps.tts: No puedo comer nada que contenga cacahuate.

steps.es: No puedo comer na' que contenga cacahuate.
steps.pt: 👂 Same warning, same kitchen. When it's this important, a server repeating it back worn-down like this is still full agreement.
steps.tts: No puedo comer na' que contenga cacahuate.

steps.pt: Fourth, and you'll hear it constantly: pues shrinks to pos, or just pus — a filler word, a small shrug.
👂 'Well, I don't know, you tell me.' The careful version — pues, fully pronounced.
👂 Same shrug, one letter shorter. You'll hear both in the same conversation, sometimes from the same person.
One more: the d between two vowels in -ado endings often disappears. Cansado becomes cansao, ocupado becomes ocupao.
None of these are mistakes — it's what relaxed, everyday Mexican Spanish sounds like, everywhere in the country.
The accent shifts by region too — central fast, coastal sing-song, Yucatán Maya-influenced, northern distinct. Expect variety, not one accent.
Back to the taco stand — same two sentences from the start, now with all four patterns in your ears.

steps.es: ¿Me da dos de pastor y uno de bistec, pa' llevar?
steps.pt: 👂 Two al pastor, one bistec, to go. Pa' is para, worn down — you already knew that one.
steps.tts: ¿Me da dos de pastor y uno de bistec, pa' llevar?

steps.pt: 👂 Right away, I'll get them ready. Ahorita — right now, or soon, depending entirely on tone.
You got it. Nothing new went in today — what changed is you can find your sentences with pieces missing.
A01 complete. Está to 'tá, para to pa', nada to na', pues to pos — four erosions over sentences you already built.

aprofundar.titulo: The ear module: why nobody speaks in this one

secoes.titulo: Recognition is a different skill from production
secoes.corpo: You can already say está, para, nada and pues correctly and in full. What this part trains is the separate skill of recognizing them worn down, at speed, in real conversation — a completely different mental task from producing a careful sentence yourself. That's why every step here is listening only.

secoes.titulo: These reductions are the norm, not an exception
secoes.corpo: 'tá, pa', na' and pos are not slang confined to one city or one social class — they are how Mexican Spanish is spoken informally almost everywhere, by almost everyone, in relaxed contexts. A traveller who only ever hears the careful, complete version has been spoken to as a visitor the entire time.

secoes.titulo: Regional variety is real — and we're not faking it
secoes.corpo: Central, coastal, Yucatecan and northern Mexican Spanish genuinely sound different from each other. We're telling you that variety exists rather than manufacturing fake regional accents with a single voice actor, which would teach you an accent that doesn't actually belong to anywhere.

permissao: You are allowed to catch one word in five and keep listening — take that word, use it, and let the rest go past. You never correct anybody for speaking this way; it isn't sloppy, it's just how the language actually moves at speed. And you will never need to talk like this yourself — understanding it is the whole job here.
espelho: Leaving a clean, complete pause at the end of your sentence is the part that can read as odd to them — there was no gap at all in what you just heard, and a pause that size often signals you're finished with the topic, so somebody else picks it up.

fichasCulturais.sinal: A vendor answers you clearly and slowly, then turns to the regular next to you and says the next thing at what feels like twice the speed.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I understood a second ago and now I understand nothing — my Spanish only works when someone is being patient with me.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Speech aimed at a visitor is often naturally slowed and fully pronounced; speech aimed at a regular customer isn't. What changed in that second was the audience, not your Spanish.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Stay in it. Count the rhythm instead of hunting for every consonant, and hold on to the one word you did catch.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You keep listening through the fast half of the conversation instead of tuning out — and the fast half is where the actual recommendation or the real answer usually lands.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not at a hotel desk, an airport counter or anywhere set up specifically to serve visitors — those run at visitor speed all day, with no faster version underneath.
